1a.html:
Given: CaO dissolved substitutionally in fluorite \mathrm{ZrO_2}, which has one \mathrm{Zr^{4+}} site for every two \mathrm{O^{2-}} sites.

Find: the defect reaction, the equilibrium constant and the defect concentration.

Solution

Step 1, defect reaction. \mathrm{Ca^{2+}} on a \mathrm{Zr^{4+}} site carries an effective charge of -2, written \mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}. CaO brings one cation but only one oxygen, while each cation site of \mathrm{ZrO_2} needs two oxygen sites. The second oxygen site stays empty as a doubly positive vacancy, which also balances the charge:

\mathrm{CaO} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{ZrO_2}\ } \mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}} + \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}

Mass: one Ca and one O on each side. Sites: one cation site to two anion sites. Charge: (-2) + 0 + (+2) = 0.

Step 2, mass-action law. With brackets as defects per \mathrm{ZrO_2} formula unit and a_{\mathrm{CaO}} the activity of the dissolving oxide:

K = \frac{[\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}]\,[\mathrm{O_O^{\times}}]\,[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}]}{a_{\mathrm{CaO}}} = \exp\left(-\frac{\Delta G}{kT}\right) = \exp\left(\frac{\Delta S}{k}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta H}{kT}\right)

The solution is dilute, so the host oxygen sites have unit activity, [\mathrm{O_O^{\times}}] \approx 1. Taking the entropy factor as 1:

K = \frac{[\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}]\,[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}]}{a_{\mathrm{CaO}}} \approx \exp\left(-\frac{\Delta H}{kT}\right)

K is dimensionless; \Delta H is the enthalpy of the whole reaction in eV and k = 8.617\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV\,K^{-1}}.

Step 3, electroneutrality. Total negative effective charge equals total positive effective charge:

2[\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] = 2[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}] \quad\Rightarrow\quad [\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] = [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}]

Step 4, solve. Substituting Step 3 into Step 2:

\begin{aligned} K\,a_{\mathrm{CaO}} &= [\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}]^2 \\ [\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] &= \left(K\,a_{\mathrm{CaO}}\right)^{1/2} \end{aligned}
\boxed{[\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] = [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}] = a_{\mathrm{CaO}}^{1/2}\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta H}{2kT}\right)}

Answer: both defects rise as a_{\mathrm{CaO}}^{1/2}, and a plot of \ln[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}] against 1/T is a straight line of slope -\Delta H/2k. Every dissolved Ca creates one oxygen vacancy, which is why CaO-stabilised zirconia is an oxygen-ion conductor for oxygen sensors and fuel cells.
pts: Correct Kroger-Vink reaction \mathrm{CaO} \to \mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}} + \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}} with \mathrm{ZrO_2} written over the arrow
Checks mass, site ratio (one cation to two anion sites) and charge, (-2) + (+2) = 0
Mass-action expression K = [\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}][\mathrm{O_O^{\times}}][\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}]/a_{\mathrm{CaO}} with [\mathrm{O_O^{\times}}] \approx 1
Writes K = \exp(-\Delta G/kT) \approx \exp(-\Delta H/kT), entropy factor taken as 1

Electroneutrality 2[\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] = 2[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}], so the two are equal per formula unit (or [\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] = 2[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}] with site fractions, convention stated)
Boxed result [\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] = a_{\mathrm{CaO}}^{1/2}\exp(-\Delta H/2kT) (or (2a_{\mathrm{CaO}})^{1/2}\exp(-\Delta H/2kT) with site fractions)
States a consequence: Arrhenius slope -\Delta H/2k, or vacancies make the material an oxygen-ion conductor
1a.src: Defects in ceramics: point defects and non-stoichiometry, slides 6-8, 12-14, 28-29; Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, pp 203-204
1a.watch:
• \mathrm{Ca^{2+}} on a \mathrm{Zr^{4+}} site is doubly negative, \mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}; putting dots on it is the commonest slip.
  • Interstitial compensation, 2\mathrm{CaO} \to \mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}} + \mathrm{Ca_i^{\bullet\bullet}} + 2\mathrm{O_O^{\times}}, also balances. The deck's density test on \mathrm{Zr_{0.85}Ca_{0.15}O_{1.85}} (calculated 5.57 for vacancies against 6.01 \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}} for interstitials) selects the vacancy model.
  • Convention: brackets here are defects per formula unit, as in the deck's Kroger-Vink diagram for CaO-doped \mathrm{ZrO_2}, where [\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] = [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}]. If brackets are site fractions of each sublattice, the two O sites per Zr site give [\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] = 2[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}] and [\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] = (2Ka_{\mathrm{CaO}})^{1/2}. The deck's YSZ example uses site fractions, hence its factor 4. Say which convention you use.
  • If \Delta H is given per defect, \Delta H^{\prime} = \Delta H/2, the exponent becomes -\Delta H^{\prime}/kT.

1b.html:
Given: a_{\mathrm{CaO}} = 0.2, \Delta H = 2.4\ \mathrm{eV} for the defect reaction, T = 1500\ \mathrm{K}, k = 8.617\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV\,K^{-1}}.

Find: the concentration of \mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}.

Solution. From part (a), \mathrm{CaO} \to \mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}} + \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}} with electroneutrality [\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] = [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}], so

\begin{aligned} [\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] &= a_{\mathrm{CaO}}^{1/2}\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta H}{2kT}\right) \\ kT &= (8.617\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV\,K^{-1}})(1500\ \mathrm{K}) = 0.1293\ \mathrm{eV} \\ \frac{\Delta H}{2kT} &= \frac{2.4\ \mathrm{eV}}{2 \times 0.1293\ \mathrm{eV}} = 9.284 \\ \exp(-9.284) &= 9.29\times10^{-5} \\ [\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] &= (0.2)^{1/2} \times 9.29\times10^{-5} = 0.447 \times 9.29\times10^{-5} = 4.15\times10^{-5} \end{aligned}

The exponent is eV over eV, so the result is a pure number: defects per \mathrm{ZrO_2} formula unit, that is per Zr site.

Answer: [\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] \approx 4.2\times10^{-5} per Zr site (about 42 ppm), equal to [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}].
pts: Uses the part (a) result with [\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] = [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}], so the concentration is a_{\mathrm{CaO}}^{1/2}\exp(-\Delta H/2kT)
Correct kT = 0.1293\ \mathrm{eV} and exponent \Delta H/2kT = 9.28
Correct factors \exp(-9.28) = 9.29\times10^{-5} and (0.2)^{1/2} = 0.447
Final answer [\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] \approx 4.2\times10^{-5} (or 5.9\times10^{-5} with site fractions, where [\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] = 2[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}])
States that it is a dimensionless fraction per Zr site, equal to the oxygen-vacancy concentration

1b.watch:
• Forgetting the square root gives 0.2\exp(-18.57) = 1.7\times10^{-9}, wrong by four orders of magnitude.
  • With the site-fraction convention of part (a), [\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] = 5.9\times10^{-5} and the vacancy site fraction is 2.9\times10^{-5}; state the convention you use.
  • Extra: per unit volume, the deck's lattice parameter for CSZ, a = 0.5131\ \mathrm{nm}, with 4 Zr per fluorite cell gives 2.96\times10^{22} Zr sites per \mathrm{cm^3}, so [\mathrm{Ca_{Zr}^{\prime\prime}}] \approx 1.2\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}.
  • This is the dilute equilibrium model the question sets. Practical CSZ has about 15 mol% CaO fixed by the batch composition, where defect interactions matter.

1c.html:
Given: \phi_{\mathrm{Pt}} = 5.65\ \mathrm{eV}, \phi_{\mathrm{Al}} = 4.28\ \mathrm{eV}, n-type \mathrm{SnO_2} with \phi_s = 6.3\ \mathrm{eV}.

Find: whether Pt/\mathrm{SnO_2} and Al/\mathrm{SnO_2} are Schottky or Ohmic.

Rule (n-type semiconductor). On contact, electrons flow from the side with the higher Fermi level (smaller work function) until the Fermi levels line up.

  • \phi_m > \phi_s: electrons leave the oxide, leaving a depletion layer of ionised donors. The bands bend up and a barrier \phi_B = \phi_m - \chi blocks the electrons: Schottky (rectifying).
  • \phi_m < \phi_s: electrons enter the oxide and form an accumulation layer. The bands bend down and there is no barrier: Ohmic.

Solution

\begin{aligned} \text{Pt/SnO}_2: \quad \phi_m - \phi_s &= 5.65 - 6.30 = -0.65\ \mathrm{eV} < 0 \\ \text{Al/SnO}_2: \quad \phi_m - \phi_s &= 4.28 - 6.30 = -2.02\ \mathrm{eV} < 0 \end{aligned}

In both pairs the metal Fermi level lies above that of \mathrm{SnO_2}, so electrons flow into the oxide. The bands bend down by 0.65 eV (Pt) and 2.02 eV (Al), and electrons cross the junction freely in either direction.

Answer: with the printed work functions both junctions are Ohmic: Pt/\mathrm{SnO_2} (accumulation of 0.65 eV) and Al/\mathrm{SnO_2} (2.02 eV, the stronger Ohmic contact). Neither gives the rectifying junction a Schottky-diode sensor needs; that would need a metal with \phi_m > 6.3\ \mathrm{eV}.
pts: States the rule for n-type: \phi_m > \phi_s gives a depletion barrier (Schottky); \phi_m < \phi_s gives accumulation (Ohmic)
Explains it by electron flow from the higher Fermi level until the Fermi levels align
Pt: 5.65 < 6.3, difference -0.65 eV, so Ohmic
Al: 4.28 < 6.3, difference -2.02 eV, so Ohmic
Band diagram with E_C bending down at the interface and no barrier
Notes that a Schottky contact on this oxide needs \phi_m > \phi_s, with barrier \phi_B = \phi_m - \chi
1c.sketch:
• Energy levels before contact: vacuum level, E_F of Al (4.28), Pt (5.65) and \mathrm{SnO_2} (6.30 eV below vacuum).
  • After contact: flat E_F; E_C of \mathrm{SnO_2} bending down at the interface, labelled "accumulation, no barrier, Ohmic".
1c.src: Ohmic versus Schottky contacts, slides 1-2; Ceramic sensors, slides 12, 15-16
1c.watch:
• The printed 6.3 eV is unusually high for \mathrm{SnO_2} (about 4.7 to 4.9 eV is typical, electron affinity about 4.5 eV). With a typical value of about 4.9 eV, Pt (5.65 > 4.9, so \phi_m > \phi_s) would form a Schottky barrier and Al (4.28 < 4.9) would stay Ohmic. This is why the sensors deck lists Pd/\mathrm{SnO_2} and Pt/\mathrm{TiO_2} as Schottky diodes. Answer with the printed data, but show that you know this.
  • For a p-type semiconductor the rule reverses: \phi_m < \phi_s is blocking.

2a.html:
Given: \mathrm{Dy_3Ga_5O_{12}} (DGG) substrate, (100), a_s = 12.405 Å; the printed lattice parameters and \lambda_{100}, \lambda_{111} of the rare-earth iron garnets \mathrm{RE_3Fe_5O_{12}}. Not printed, so assumed: typical garnet elastic constants E \approx 200 GPa, \nu \approx 0.29.

Find: the garnet film most likely to be magnetised out of plane.

Solution

Step 1, strain from the misfit. A thin epitaxial film takes the substrate's in-plane spacing, so it carries a biaxial strain and stress

\varepsilon = \frac{a_s - a_f}{a_f}, \qquad \sigma = \frac{E}{1 - \nu}\,\varepsilon \approx 2.8\times10^{11}\,\varepsilon\ \mathrm{Pa}

A film smaller than the substrate (a_f < a_s) is in tension (\varepsilon > 0); a larger one is compressed.

Step 2, magnetoelastic anisotropy of a (100) film. The film normal is a cube axis, so \lambda_{100} governs. With K > 0 meaning the normal is easy:

K_{me} = -\tfrac{3}{2}\lambda_{100}\,\sigma

Out-of-plane anisotropy needs \lambda_{100}\varepsilon < 0: a compressed film needs \lambda_{100} > 0, a film in tension \lambda_{100} < 0. K_{me} must also beat the film's shape anisotropy, \mu_0 M_s^2/2 \approx 1.2\times10^4\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}} for YIG (M_s \approx 140\ \mathrm{kA\,m^{-1}}).

Step 3, screen the table (\lambda in 10^{-6}):

REa_f (Å)\varepsilon (%)\lambda_{100}K_{me} (\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}})Out of plane?
Y12.376+0.23−1.25+1.2\times10^{3}weak
Sm12.530−1.00+21+8.9\times10^{4}strong
Eu12.498−0.74+21+6.6\times10^{4}strong
Gd12.470−0.52+0.2+4\times10^{2}negligible
Tb12.436−0.25−3.3-3.5\times10^{3}no
Dy12.4050−12.50no strain
Ho12.375+0.24−4.0+4.1\times10^{3}weak
Er, Tm, Yb12.349 to 12.302+0.45 to +0.84+2, +1.4, +1.4-3.8 to -5.0\times10^{3}no

Step 4, choose. Only Sm and Eu combine a large \lambda_{100} (+21\times10^{-6}) with the right strain: both cells are larger than DGG, so the films are compressed. EuIG has the smaller misfit (0.74 % against 1.0 %), so it is more likely to grow coherently; the critical thickness for misfit dislocations falls as the misfit rises.

Answer: grow a thin (a few tens of nm), coherently strained \mathrm{Eu_3Fe_5O_{12}} film on DGG (100): compressive strain 0.74 %, \lambda_{100} = +21\times10^{-6}, K_{me} \approx +6.6\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}, about five times the shape anisotropy, so the easy axis is the film normal. \mathrm{Sm_3Fe_5O_{12}} would give even more (8.9\times10^4\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}) if it stays coherent at 1 % misfit; an (Eu,Sm) garnet can tune between them.
pts: Film takes the substrate spacing: \varepsilon = (a_s - a_f)/a_f, tension when a_f < a_s, compression when a_f > a_s
(100) film, so \lambda_{100} applies: K_{me} = -\frac{3}{2}\lambda_{100}\sigma with \sigma = E\varepsilon/(1 - \nu)
Out of plane needs \lambda_{100}\varepsilon < 0 (compression with \lambda_{100} > 0, tension with \lambda_{100} < 0) and K_{me} > \mu_0 M_s^2/2
Screens the table with correct misfits, for example Sm -1.0 %, Eu -0.74 %, Tb -0.25 %, Ho +0.24 %, Tm +0.65 %, Dy 0
Selects EuIG (or SmIG): \lambda_{100} = +21\times10^{-6} under compression, K_{me} \approx 6.6\times10^4 (Eu) or 8.9\times10^4 (Sm) \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}
Justifies with coherence: the smaller misfit keeps the film strained; film kept below the critical thickness
Rejects the wrong-sign films (Tb, Er, Tm, Yb) and the unstrained DyIG
2a.src: Magnetic anisotropy, p 2; Lecture 03 Magnetic ceramics, slides 45, 56; O'Handley, Modern Magnetic Materials, pp 263-265, 293, 652-654, 669
2a.watch:
• The elastic constants are not printed, so the K_{me} values are estimates; the sign rule and the ranking do not depend on them.
  • DyIG has a large negative \lambda_{100} (-12.5\times10^{-6}) but no strain on this substrate, because the printed DGG value equals the DyIG entry, so it gains no magnetoelastic anisotropy. Real DGG is smaller (about 12.31 Å; a gallium garnet is about 0.09 Å smaller than the iron garnet of the same rare earth, compare GGG 12.383 and GdIG 12.470 Å), but use the printed value.
  • Garnets have a small negative K_1 (YIG about -6\times10^2\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}), so the [100] normal is a slightly hard crystal direction; K_{me} outweighs it by far.
  • Thermal-expansion mismatch on cooling from the growth temperature adds strain; the lattice-misfit strain dominates here.

2b.html:
Given: \mathrm{NiFe_2O_4}, cubic spinel, a = 0.84\ \mathrm{nm}, 8 formula units per cell; \mu_B = 9.27\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{A\,m^2} (printed).

Find: the net moment per formula unit with \mathrm{Ni^{2+}} all on A, and all on B.

Solution

Step 1, ionic moments (spin only, orbital moment quenched by the crystal field). \mathrm{Ni^{2+}} is 3d^8 with 2 unpaired spins, 2\,\mu_B; \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} is 3d^5 with 5 unpaired spins, 5\,\mu_B.

Step 2, coupling. Each formula unit has one A (tetrahedral) and two B (octahedral) cations. The A-O-B superexchange (125^\circ) is the strongest and is antiferromagnetic, so the net moment is

n_B = M_B - M_A

Step 3, Ni on A (normal spinel), (\mathrm{Ni})_A[\mathrm{Fe_2}]_B\mathrm{O_4}:

n_B = 2(5) - 2 = 8\,\mu_B\ \text{per formula unit}

Step 4, Ni on B (inverse spinel), (\mathrm{Fe})_A[\mathrm{NiFe}]_B\mathrm{O_4}: the two \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} cancel,

n_B = (2 + 5) - 5 = 2\,\mu_B\ \text{per formula unit}

Step 5, magnetisation with V = a^3 = (0.84\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m})^3 = 5.93\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{m^3}:

\begin{aligned} M_s &= \frac{8\,n_B\,\mu_B}{a^3} \\ \text{normal: } M_s &= \frac{8(8)(9.27\times10^{-24})}{5.93\times10^{-28}} = 1.00\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}} \\ \text{inverse: } M_s &= \frac{8(2)(9.27\times10^{-24})}{5.93\times10^{-28}} = 2.50\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}} \end{aligned}

Answer: Ni on A: 8\,\mu_B per formula unit (M_s \approx 1.0 MA/m); Ni on B: 2\,\mu_B per formula unit (M_s \approx 250 kA/m). Real \mathrm{NiFe_2O_4} is inverse, as the strong octahedral preference of \mathrm{Ni^{2+}} (crystal-field stabilisation) requires, and its measured moment is close to 2\,\mu_B.
pts: Spin-only moments \mathrm{Ni^{2+}} (3d^8) 2\,\mu_B and \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} (3d^5) 5\,\mu_B
A and B sublattices antiparallel through A-O-B superexchange, so n_B = M_B - M_A
Ni on A (normal): n_B = 10 - 2 = 8\,\mu_B per formula unit
Ni on B (inverse): \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} moments cancel, n_B = 2\,\mu_B per formula unit
Converts with M_s = 8n_B\mu_B/a^3: about 1.0 MA/m and 250 kA/m
Notes that real \mathrm{NiFe_2O_4} is inverse (octahedral preference of \mathrm{Ni^{2+}})
2b.src: Lecture 03 Magnetic ceramics, slides 29, 36-39; Magnetic lecture 1, slides 33-35; Superexchange, pp 4-5
2b.watch:
• Adding the moments instead of subtracting them gives 12\,\mu_B for both distributions and ignores the antiparallel A and B sublattices.
  • The lattice parameter is not needed for the moment per formula unit; it is used only for M_s in A/m, which part (c) needs.
  • The measured moment of \mathrm{NiFe_2O_4} is about 2.2 to 2.3\,\mu_B because \mathrm{Ni^{2+}} keeps a small orbital moment (g \approx 2.2).

2c.html:
Given: measured M_s = 300\ \mathrm{kA\,m^{-1}}; from part (b), a = 0.84\ \mathrm{nm}, 8 formula units per cell, \mu_B = 9.27\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{A\,m^2}, \mathrm{Ni^{2+}} 2\,\mu_B, \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} 5\,\mu_B.

Find: the fraction of \mathrm{Ni^{2+}} on A and on B sites.

Solution

Step 1, moment per formula unit from the measurement:

n_B = \frac{M_s a^3}{8\mu_B} = \frac{(3.00\times10^{5})(5.927\times10^{-28})}{8(9.27\times10^{-24})} = 2.40\,\mu_B

This lies between the inverse (2\,\mu_B) and normal (8\,\mu_B) limits, so the spinel is partly inverse.

Step 2, mixed distribution. Let a fraction \delta of the Ni sit on A; the displaced \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} goes to B:

(\mathrm{Ni}_{\delta}\mathrm{Fe}_{1-\delta})_A[\mathrm{Ni}_{1-\delta}\mathrm{Fe}_{1+\delta}]_B\mathrm{O_4}
\begin{aligned} M_A &= 2\delta + 5(1-\delta) = 5 - 3\delta \\ M_B &= 2(1-\delta) + 5(1+\delta) = 7 + 3\delta \\ n_B &= M_B - M_A = 2 + 6\delta \end{aligned}

Check: \delta = 0 gives 2 and \delta = 1 gives 8, as in part (b).

Step 3, solve:

2 + 6\delta = 2.40 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \delta = \frac{0.40}{6} = 0.066

Answer: about 6.6% of the \mathrm{Ni^{2+}} on A sites and 93.4% on B sites, (\mathrm{Ni_{0.066}Fe_{0.934}})_A[\mathrm{Ni_{0.934}Fe_{1.066}}]_B\mathrm{O_4} (degree of inversion 0.93). Each Ni moved to A swaps with an \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} and raises the net moment by 6\,\mu_B, so a small amount of disorder explains the extra 0.4\,\mu_B.
pts: Converts M_s to moment per formula unit with n_B = M_s a^3/(8\mu_B)
Obtains n_B \approx 2.4\,\mu_B per formula unit, between the inverse and normal limits
Writes the mixed distribution (\mathrm{Ni}_\delta\mathrm{Fe}_{1-\delta})_A[\mathrm{Ni}_{1-\delta}\mathrm{Fe}_{1+\delta}]_B\mathrm{O_4}
Derives n_B = (7 + 3\delta) - (5 - 3\delta) = 2 + 6\delta
Solves \delta \approx 0.066: about 7% of Ni on A and 93% on B
2c.src: Lecture 03 Magnetic ceramics, slides 36-41; Superexchange, pp 5-8
2c.watch:
• Keep the Fe count right: every Ni that goes to A sends one \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} to B, so B holds \mathrm{Fe}_{1+\delta}.
  • Another honest reading: the extra 0.4\,\mu_B could come from the orbital moment of \mathrm{Ni^{2+}} (measured \mathrm{NiFe_2O_4} gives about 2.3\,\mu_B even when fully inverse). The question asks for the distribution, so give \delta and mention this.
  • The model treats 300 kA/m as the full (0 K) saturation value. If it was measured at room temperature, the 0 K moment is higher and \delta = 0.066 is a lower bound.

3a.html:
Given: a cubic oxide with K_1 < 0 and K_2 < 0, both non-zero.

Find: the magnetocrystalline energy with \mathbf{M} along [100], [110] and [111].

Solution. Spin-orbit coupling ties \mathbf{M} to the orbitals, which the crystal field locks to the lattice, so the energy depends on the direction of \mathbf{M} relative to the cube axes. The lowest terms allowed by cubic symmetry (equation sheet), with \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3 the direction cosines of \mathbf{M}:

E = K_0 + K_1\left(\alpha_1^2\alpha_2^2 + \alpha_2^2\alpha_3^2 + \alpha_3^2\alpha_1^2\right) + K_2\,\alpha_1^2\alpha_2^2\alpha_3^2
\mathbf{M} along\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3K_1 bracketK_2 productEnergy
[100]1, 0, 000E_{100} = K_0
[110]\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, 0\tfrac{1}{4}0E_{110} = K_0 + \tfrac{1}{4}K_1
[111]\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}3 \times \tfrac{1}{9} = \tfrac{1}{3}\tfrac{1}{27}E_{111} = K_0 + \tfrac{1}{3}K_1 + \tfrac{1}{27}K_2

Ranking. With both constants negative:

E_{110} - E_{100} = \frac{K_1}{4} < 0, \qquad E_{111} - E_{110} = \frac{K_1}{12} + \frac{K_2}{27} < 0

Answer: E_{100} = K_0, E_{110} = K_0 + K_1/4 and E_{111} = K_0 + K_1/3 + K_2/27, so E_{111} < E_{110} < E_{100}. The \langle 111\rangle body diagonals are the easy axes, \langle 110\rangle is intermediate and \langle 100\rangle is hard, as in nickel and most spinel ferrites. With the values of part (b), K_1 = -1\times10^4 and K_2 = -2\times10^4\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}, [110] lies 2.5\times10^3 and [111] lies 4.07\times10^3\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}} below [100].
pts: Writes the cubic energy E = K_0 + K_1(\alpha_1^2\alpha_2^2 + \alpha_2^2\alpha_3^2 + \alpha_3^2\alpha_1^2) + K_2\alpha_1^2\alpha_2^2\alpha_3^2 in direction cosines
[100]: \alpha = (1, 0, 0), both terms vanish, E = K_0
[110]: \alpha = (1/\sqrt{2}, 1/\sqrt{2}, 0), E = K_0 + K_1/4
[111]: every \alpha_i^2 = 1/3, E = K_0 + K_1/3 + K_2/27
Ranks them for K_1, K_2 < 0: E_{111} < E_{110} < E_{100}, so \langle 111\rangle easy and \langle 100\rangle hard
3a.src: Lecture 03 Magnetic ceramics, slides 54, 56, 61; Anisotropy and domain walls, slide 4; Magnetic anisotropy, p 1
3a.watch:
• At [111] the K_1 bracket is 3 \times (1/3)(1/3) = 1/3 and the K_2 product is (1/3)^3 = 1/27; writing 1/9 for either is the usual slip.
  • K_0 does not depend on direction; only the differences between directions decide the easy axis.
  • A negative K_2 deepens the [111] minimum. With K_1 < 0, only a large positive K_2 (above 9\lvert K_1\rvert/4) would make \langle 110\rangle easy instead.

3b.fix: Slides 5 and 6 of 435-aniso write K_{\mathrm{shape}} = 0.5(N_x - N_z)M_s^2. In SI units the shape anisotropy is (\mu_0/2)(N_x - N_z)M_s^2, as the exam's equation sheet and 435-mag3 slide 56 print. The slide form holds only in Gaussian units, where the factors add up to 4\pi, while the same slide gives N = 1/3 for a sphere. Without \mu_0 this rod would give 1.6\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}} instead of 1.98\times10^4\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.
3b.html:
Given: the cubic oxide of part (a) cut into a rod with its long axis along [100] (x), N_x = 0.1; K_1 = -1\times10^4\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}, K_2 = -2\times10^4\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}, M_s = 300\ \mathrm{kA\,m^{-1}}, \mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}.

Find: the total anisotropy energy and the easy axis.

Solution

Step 1, demagnetising factors. N_x + N_y + N_z = 1, and a rod of round section has equal transverse factors:

N_y = N_z = \frac{1 - 0.1}{2} = 0.45

Step 2, total anisotropy energy = magnetocrystalline + shape (magnetostatic). With \phi the angle between \mathbf{M} and the rod axis, so that \alpha_1 = \cos\phi:

\begin{aligned} E &= K_1\left(\alpha_1^2\alpha_2^2 + \alpha_2^2\alpha_3^2 + \alpha_3^2\alpha_1^2\right) + K_2\,\alpha_1^2\alpha_2^2\alpha_3^2 + \frac{\mu_0 M_s^2}{2}\left(N_x\alpha_1^2 + N_y\alpha_2^2 + N_z\alpha_3^2\right) \\ &= \mathrm{const} + K_1\left(\alpha_1^2\alpha_2^2 + \alpha_2^2\alpha_3^2 + \alpha_3^2\alpha_1^2\right) + K_2\,\alpha_1^2\alpha_2^2\alpha_3^2 + K_{sh}\sin^2\phi \\ K_{sh} &= \frac{\mu_0 M_s^2}{2}\left(N_y - N_x\right) \end{aligned}

This is the sheet's K_{\mathrm{shape}} = (\mu_0 M_s^2/2)(N_x - N_z) with the long axis now called x. The shape term is the stray-field (magnetostatic) energy: magnetised across the rod, the long sides carry poles and a large demagnetising field H_d = -NM, so the long axis is favoured.

Step 3, numbers.

\begin{aligned} \frac{\mu_0 M_s^2}{2} &= \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(3.0\times10^{5})^2}{2} = 5.65\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}} \\ K_{sh} &= (5.65\times10^{4})(0.45 - 0.10) = 1.98\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}} \end{aligned}

Step 4, energy of each candidate direction (constant dropped):

\mathbf{M} alongcrystal term (\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}})\sin^2\phiE (\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}})
[100], rod axis000
[110]K_1/4 = -25001/2+7.4\times10^{3}
[111]K_1/3 + K_2/27 = -40742/3+9.1\times10^{3}
[011]K_1/4 = -25001+1.73\times10^{4}
[010], [001]01+1.98\times10^{4}

Step 5, is [100] a true minimum? For a small tilt the crystal term is about K_1\sin^2\phi, so

E \approx (K_1 + K_{sh})\sin^2\phi = (-1.0 + 1.98)\times10^{4}\sin^2\phi = 9.8\times10^{3}\sin^2\phi\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}} > 0

Answer: the easy axis is the rod axis [100] (either sense), with an effective uniaxial anisotropy of about 9.8\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}. The shape anisotropy, 1.98\times10^4\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}, outweighs the crystal's preference for \langle 111\rangle, which lies only 4.07\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}} below [100].

K_{sh} = (\mu_0 M_s^2/2)(N_\perp - N_\parallel), positive, so the rod axis is favoured
\mu_0 M_s^2/2 = 5.65\times10^4 and K_{sh} = 1.98\times10^4\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}
Energies relative to [100]: [110] +7.4\times10^3, [111] +9.1\times10^3, [010] +1.98\times10^4\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}
Easy axis [100], the rod axis: shape beats the \langle 111\rangle preference of the crystal
Shows that [100] is a minimum: K_1 + K_{sh} \approx 9.8\times10^3\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}} > 0

3b.watch:
• Here N_x is the factor along the rod. The sheet names the long axis z, so use N_\perp - N_\parallel; swapping them makes K_{sh} negative and the rod axis hard, which is unphysical.
  • Comparing only [100] and [111] is the method of 435-mag3 slide 61, but list [110] as well: with the rod along [100], [110] (7.4\times10^3) lies below [111] (9.1\times10^3).
  • The demagnetising factor of a real cylinder is not uniform; the uniform N of an ellipsoid of revolution is the slide's assumption.

3c.html:
Energy. With the rod along [110], the shape term is measured from [110]: E = K_1(\alpha_1^2\alpha_2^2 + \alpha_2^2\alpha_3^2 + \alpha_3^2\alpha_1^2) + K_2\alpha_1^2\alpha_2^2\alpha_3^2 + K_{sh}\sin^2\phi, with K_{sh} = (\mu_0 M_s^2/2)(N_\perp - N_\parallel).

The crystal alone cannot do it. For K_1 < 0, \langle 110\rangle is the cubic easy axis only when K_2 > 9\lvert K_1\rvert/4. Here K_2 < 0, so the crystal prefers \langle 111\rangle, and [110] can become easy only through the shape term.

Condition 1, [110] below the other axes.

\begin{aligned} E_{110} &= \tfrac{1}{4}K_1, \qquad E_{111} = \tfrac{1}{3}K_1 + \tfrac{1}{27}K_2 + \tfrac{1}{3}K_{sh}, \qquad E_{100} = \tfrac{1}{2}K_{sh} \\ E_{110} < E_{111} &\iff K_{sh} > -\left(\frac{K_1}{4} + \frac{K_2}{9}\right) = 4.7\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}} \end{aligned}

E_{110} < E_{100} holds for any K_{sh} > 0 because K_1 < 0.

Condition 2, no tilt out of [110]. Tilting by a small angle \psi towards [001], through [111]:

E \approx \tfrac{1}{4}K_1 + \left(K_{sh} + \tfrac{1}{2}K_1 + \tfrac{1}{4}K_2\right)\psi^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad K_{sh} > -\left(\frac{K_1}{2} + \frac{K_2}{4}\right) = 1.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}

Tilting in the (001) plane costs (K_{sh} - K_1)\psi^2, always positive. Condition 2 is the stricter one; between 4.7\times10^3 and 1.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}, \mathbf{M} sits between [110] and [111].

In terms of shape, with \mu_0 M_s^2/2 = 5.65\times10^4\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}:

N_\perp - N_\parallel > \frac{1.0\times10^{4}}{5.65\times10^{4}} = 0.18, \qquad N_\parallel < 0.22 \ \text{for a round rod}

Answer: the easy axis lies along [110] when the shape anisotropy exceeds -(K_1/2 + K_2/4) = 1.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}, that is N_\perp - N_\parallel > 0.18 (rod at least about 1.6 times as long as it is wide). The rod of part (b) cut along [110] (K_{sh} = 1.98\times10^4\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}) qualifies.
pts: Writes the total energy with the shape term measured from the rod axis [110]
States that the crystal alone cannot make [110] easy: it needs K_1 < 0 with K_2 > 9\lvert K_1\rvert/4, impossible for K_2 < 0
Compares [110] with [111]: K_{sh} > -(K_1/4 + K_2/9) = 4.7\times10^3\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}; [100] always lies higher
Stability against tilting towards [111]: K_{sh} > -(K_1/2 + K_2/4) = 1.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}, the binding condition
Converts with M_s = 300\ \mathrm{kA\,m^{-1}}: N_\perp - N_\parallel > 0.18, or N_\parallel < 0.22 for a round rod
Concludes that the part (b) rod (K_{sh} = 1.98\times10^4\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}) has its easy axis along [110]

3c.watch:
• Comparing only the three principal axes gives 4.7\times10^3\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}. That is necessary but not sufficient: below 1.0\times10^4, \mathbf{M} settles at an intermediate direction between [110] and [111]. A scan of all directions confirms the 1.0\times10^4 limit.
  • The aspect ratio of about 1.6 assumes a prolate ellipsoid; a cylinder of the same N_\parallel is slightly shorter.
  • Stresses add a magnetoelastic term and can shift the condition; the question assumes a stress-free rod.

4a.html:
Given: a magnetoelastic sphere with normal strains e_z along z and e_x = e_y = -e_z/2, no shear strains; x, y, z taken along the cube axes.

Find: an expression for the magnetoelastic anisotropy K_{me}.

Solution

Step 1, magnetoelastic energy (equation sheet). With no shear strains the B_2 term vanishes:

u_{me} = B_1\left(\alpha_1^2 e_x + \alpha_2^2 e_y + \alpha_3^2 e_z\right)

Step 2, substitute the strains. With \theta the angle between \mathbf{M} and z, \alpha_3^2 = \cos^2\theta and \alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2 = \sin^2\theta:

\begin{aligned} u_{me} &= B_1 e_z\left(\cos^2\theta - \tfrac{1}{2}\sin^2\theta\right) = B_1 e_z\left(1 - \tfrac{3}{2}\sin^2\theta\right) \\ &= B_1 e_z - \tfrac{3}{2}B_1 e_z\sin^2\theta \end{aligned}

Step 3, compare with the uniaxial form u = K_0 + K_{me}\sin^2\theta:

\boxed{K_{me} = -\tfrac{3}{2}B_1 e_z}

Step 4, in terms of magnetostriction. With \lambda_{100} = -\tfrac{2}{3}B_1/(c_{11} - c_{12}), and since \sigma_z - \sigma_x = (c_{11} - c_{12})(e_z - e_x) = \tfrac{3}{2}(c_{11} - c_{12})e_z:

K_{me} = \tfrac{9}{4}\lambda_{100}\left(c_{11} - c_{12}\right)e_z = \tfrac{3}{2}\lambda_{100}\left(\sigma_z - \sigma_x\right)

Answer: K_{me} = -\frac{3}{2}B_1 e_z = \frac{9}{4}\lambda_{100}(c_{11} - c_{12})e_z, a uniaxial anisotropy about the stretch axis z. The stretch axis is easy when K_{me} > 0, that is B_1 e_z < 0: a material with \lambda_{100} > 0 stretched along z magnetises along z, and one with \lambda_{100} < 0 prefers the xy plane. The elastic energy of an imposed strain does not depend on the direction of \mathbf{M}, and a sphere has N = 1/3 on every axis, so it has no shape anisotropy: K_{me} is the whole uniaxial term, added to the cubic crystal anisotropy.
pts: Magnetoelastic energy u_{me} = B_1(\alpha_1^2 e_x + \alpha_2^2 e_y + \alpha_3^2 e_z), with the B_2 term zero (no shear strain)
Substitutes e_x = e_y = -e_z/2 and \alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2 = \sin^2\theta: u_{me} = B_1 e_z(\cos^2\theta - \frac{1}{2}\sin^2\theta)
Rearranges to u_{me} = B_1 e_z - \frac{3}{2}B_1 e_z\sin^2\theta
K_{me} = -\frac{3}{2}B_1 e_z, uniaxial about z
Magnetostriction form K_{me} = \frac{9}{4}\lambda_{100}(c_{11} - c_{12})e_z or \frac{3}{2}\lambda_{100}(\sigma_z - \sigma_x)
Sign: z easy when B_1 e_z < 0 (\lambda_{100} > 0 in tension); a sphere adds no shape anisotropy
4a.src: Magnetic anisotropy, p 2; Anisotropy and domain walls, slide 6; O'Handley, Modern Magnetic Materials, pp 257, 263-265
4a.watch:
• The strain is volume conserving (e_x + e_y + e_z = 0), so the isotropic part of the magnetoelastic energy drops out and only the \sin^2\theta term remains.
  • Keep the sign convention explicit: with u = K\sin^2\theta, a positive K_{me} makes z easy.
  • For an elastically isotropic polycrystal replace \lambda_{100} by \lambda_s and c_{11} - c_{12} by 2G: K_{me} = \frac{9}{2}\lambda_s G e_z, the same as \frac{3}{2}\lambda_s\sigma for this stress state.

4b.html:
Given: a cubic magnetoelastic material with B_1 = 0 and B_2 \neq 0.

Find: the strain along [100] for \mathbf{M} along [001] and along [111].

Solution. Strain along a direction with cosines \beta_i, for \mathbf{M} with cosines \alpha_i (equation sheet):

\frac{\delta l}{l} = -\frac{B_1}{c_{11} - c_{12}}\left(\alpha_1^2\beta_1^2 + \alpha_2^2\beta_2^2 + \alpha_3^2\beta_3^2 - \tfrac{1}{3}\right) - \frac{B_2}{c_{44}}\left(\alpha_1\alpha_2\beta_1\beta_2 + \alpha_2\alpha_3\beta_2\beta_3 + \alpha_3\alpha_1\beta_3\beta_1\right)

With B_1 = 0 only the B_2 (shear) term is left. Along [100], \beta = (1, 0, 0), so every product \beta_i\beta_j with i \neq j is zero.

M along [001], \alpha = (0, 0, 1): the products \alpha_i\alpha_j are zero as well, so \delta l/l = 0.

M along [111], \alpha_i = 1/\sqrt{3}: each \alpha_i\alpha_j = 1/3, but it multiplies \beta_i\beta_j = 0:

\frac{\delta l}{l} = -\frac{B_2}{c_{44}}\left[\tfrac{1}{3}(1)(0) + \tfrac{1}{3}(0)(0) + \tfrac{1}{3}(0)(1)\right] = 0

Answer: the strain along [100] is zero in both cases. B_1 = 0 means \lambda_{100} = -\frac{2}{3}B_1/(c_{11} - c_{12}) = 0: the cube edges never change length. B_2 produces only shear strains, e_{ij} = -B_2\alpha_i\alpha_j/c_{44}. With \mathbf{M} along [001] there is no strain at all; with \mathbf{M} along [111] the cube distorts rhombohedrally, its right angles change by -B_2/(3c_{44}), yet its edges keep their length. The effect appears along [111] instead: \delta l/l = -B_2/(3c_{44}) = \lambda_{111}.
pts: Uses the strain formula with B_1 = 0, so only the B_2 shear term remains
Along [100], \beta = (1, 0, 0), so every \beta_i\beta_j (i \neq j) is zero
\mathbf{M} along [001]: \delta l/l = 0 (all \alpha_i\alpha_j are zero too)
\mathbf{M} along [111]: \alpha_i\alpha_j = 1/3 multiplies \beta_i\beta_j = 0, so \delta l/l = 0
Explains: \lambda_{100} = 0, B_2 gives only shear (rhombohedral) strain, seen along [111] as \lambda_{111} = -B_2/(3c_{44})
4b.src: Magnetic anisotropy, p 3; O'Handley, Modern Magnetic Materials, pp 257-262, 294
4b.watch:
• Do not use \lambda_{111} for "M along [111]": the measuring direction is [100], and the \beta products decide.
  • The sheet's B_2 term uses engineering shear strains; that is why \lambda_{111} = -B_2/(3c_{44}) has no factor 2.
  • The isotropic volume (forced) magnetostriction is left out, as on the equation sheet.

4c.html:
Reading Figure 01 (Pd-doped \mathrm{SnO_2}). Each gas peaks where its surface oxidation by \mathrm{O^-} is fast but the gas still reaches the grain interior. From the figure: \mathrm{H_2} peaks at about 160^\circ\mathrm{C}, \mathrm{C_3H_8} at about 260^\circ\mathrm{C} and \mathrm{CH_4} at about 340^\circ\mathrm{C} (stable C-H bonds need heat). CO is highest near room temperature and exceeds \mathrm{H_2} only below about 45^\circ\mathrm{C}; above 100^\circ\mathrm{C} it is almost zero, because Pd burns CO on the surface.

Design strategy

  1. Measure CO at low temperature, about 30 to 45^\circ\mathrm{C}. Here CO gives the largest signal and propane and methane give none. Pd makes this possible by spilling activated oxygen onto \mathrm{SnO_2}.
  2. Remove the \mathrm{H_2} error. A second element, or a second step of the same element, at about 160^\circ\mathrm{C} sees \mathrm{H_2} almost alone, since CO is near zero there. Subtract its scaled signal from the low-temperature reading (a temperature-modulated array with data analysis).
  3. Temperature cycling. A short pulse at 300 to 400^\circ\mathrm{C} before each reading burns off adsorbed water and hydroxyls and resets the baseline; the reading is then taken during the cool step.
  4. Raise sensitivity. Use nanocrystalline, porous \mathrm{SnO_2} with grain size at most twice the depletion depth, so CO changes the conduction of whole grains. Keep the Pd finely dispersed over the grains.
  5. Filter. A porous charcoal or zeolite overlayer removes heavier hydrocarbons and solvent vapours.

Report the signal as S = \Delta R/R_a and calibrate it against CO concentration.
pts: Reads Figure 01: peaks of \mathrm{H_2} (about 160^\circ\mathrm{C}), \mathrm{C_3H_8} (about 260^\circ\mathrm{C}), \mathrm{CH_4} (about 340^\circ\mathrm{C}); CO largest near room temperature
Chooses a low operating temperature (below about 50^\circ\mathrm{C}) where CO exceeds \mathrm{H_2} and the hydrocarbons give no signal
Corrects for \mathrm{H_2} with a second reading at the \mathrm{H_2} peak (sensor array or temperature modulation with data analysis)
Uses temperature cycling: a high-temperature cleaning pulse, then measurement at low temperature
Raises sensitivity with nanosized grains (about 2\times the depletion depth or less) and a porous film, explained by the depletion layer
Uses the Pd catalyst (or another selective catalyst) to promote CO oxidation at low temperature
Adds a filter or membrane against interfering hydrocarbons
4c.watch:
• A common wrong reading is to run the sensor at 350 to 400^\circ\mathrm{C} because the CO label sits there; the CO curve there is the flat dotted line near zero.
  • The values above are read from a schematic figure, so give them as approximate.
  • Commercial CO sensors on \mathrm{SnO_2} use exactly this two-step heater cycle: a hot cleaning step and a cool measuring step.

4d.html:
Temperature alone gives only partial selectivity:

  1. Overlapping curves. The peaks are broad; near 40^\circ\mathrm{C} \mathrm{H_2} still responds almost as much as CO.
  2. Identity against concentration. One resistance change cannot tell a little \mathrm{H_2} from a lot of CO.
  3. Weak, slow signal. At the selective low temperature CO sensitivity is small and response and recovery are slow.
  4. Drift. Humidity, ageing and poisoning (\mathrm{SO_x}, soot) shift the peaks and the baseline.
  5. Heater control. The oxide's own resistance depends on T, so heater or ambient changes look like gas and need recalibration.

Hence catalysts, filters and sensor arrays are added.
pts: Broad, overlapping response curves: no temperature where only CO responds
One signal cannot separate gas identity from concentration
The selective temperature gives low sensitivity and slow response or recovery
Drift: humidity, ageing or poisoning shift the curves and the baseline
Temperature dependence of the baseline itself, so heater or ambient changes cause false signals and need calibration

5a.fix: Slide 21 says the first commercially operated high-speed superconducting maglev opened in Shanghai in 2004. The Shanghai line (Transrapid) uses conventional, non-superconducting electromagnets that attract the train up to a steel rail with a gap of about 10 mm (electromagnetic suspension). Superconducting maglev (the Japanese system) has run on test lines and is being built for the Chuo Shinkansen.
5a.html:
A maglev train is lifted, guided and driven by magnetic forces with no wheel-rail contact (slides 20-22). Superconductors make this practical in two ways.

1. Superconducting magnets (zero resistance). NbTi coils on the train, cooled to about 4 K, run in persistent-current mode: once charged, the current circulates with no loss (slide 3), giving fields of several tesla from light, iron-free coils with no power supply.

  • Levitation (electrodynamic): as the train moves, these fields induce currents in normal-metal figure-of-eight coils in the guideway sidewalls. By Lenz's law their field opposes the onboard magnets and lifts the train about 10 cm (slide 20), once it passes about 150 km/h (it runs on wheels below that).
  • Guidance: the coils on the two sidewalls are cross-connected, so a sideways shift creates a restoring force.
  • Propulsion and braking: guideway coils fed with three-phase AC form a linear synchronous motor with the onboard magnets; reversing the travelling field brakes the train and returns energy.

2. Bulk high-T_c superconductors (Meissner effect and flux pinning). YBCO blocks (T_c = 92 K) cooled by liquid nitrogen on the vehicle, over a permanent-magnet track, expel and pin the field. They lift and centre the vehicle passively, even at rest, with no control power.

Contribution to efficiency

  • No friction or wear: low maintenance and very high speed (581 km/h in 2003, 603 km/h in 2015).
  • No resistive loss in the magnets; only the cryocoolers draw power.
  • A large gap (about 10 cm, against about 1 cm for conventional electromagnetic maglev) tolerates guideway errors without active gap control.
  • Light coils reduce vehicle mass and energy per seat.
  • Ceramic superconductors can be cooled by cheap liquid nitrogen at 77 K instead of liquid helium (slide 23).

Limits: cryogenic plant and quench risk, magnetic drag at low speed, shielding of passengers from the field, and a costly guideway.
pts: Maglev principle: levitation, guidance and propulsion by magnetic forces without contact
Zero resistance allows persistent-current superconducting magnets (NbTi, about 4 K) with strong fields, no power supply and no loss
Electrodynamic levitation: moving SC magnets induce opposing currents in guideway coils (Lenz); gap about 10 cm; wheels at low speed
Guidance by cross-connected sidewall coils
Propulsion and braking by a linear synchronous motor (AC guideway coils with onboard magnets)
Bulk YBCO levitation by the Meissner effect and flux pinning: passive, stable even at rest, liquid-nitrogen cooled
Efficiency: no friction or wear, no resistive magnet loss, large gap, light vehicle, speeds above 500 km/h (any three with reasons, 1 each)
Limits: cryogenics, quench risk, low-speed drag, field shielding or cost
5a.watch:
• Do not say the Shanghai line is superconducting (see Correction); it is the standard example of conventional electromagnetic maglev.
  • The large lift of the superconducting system appears only with motion; the Meissner and flux-pinning systems lift at standstill.
  • The operating Japanese system uses low-temperature NbTi coils; high-temperature coils cooled at higher temperature have been tested but cost and quench protection remain issues.

5b.fix: Figure 02 labels the composition axis "\mathrm{Y_2O_3} (mol%)". The same diagram on 435-mech slides 13 and 15 is plotted in mol% \mathrm{YO_{1.5}}, and only that scale fits practice: fully stabilised zirconia (8 mol% \mathrm{Y_2O_3}) is 14.8 on it, near the cubic boundary, and 3 mol% \mathrm{Y_2O_3} is 5.8. Convert with mol% \mathrm{Y_2O_3} = 100x/(200 - x), where x is the axis reading. The design above is drawn on the figure as printed and quoted in both units.
5b.html:
Why pure \mathrm{ZrO_2} is not tough. Pure zirconia has three polymorphs (Figure 02): monoclinic (m) up to about 1170^\circ\mathrm{C}, tetragonal (t) up to about 2370^\circ\mathrm{C}, cubic (c) above. A part sintered at 1400 to 1600^\circ\mathrm{C} is tetragonal. On cooling it turns monoclinic (near 950^\circ\mathrm{C}, with hysteresis) by a martensitic, diffusionless shear with a large volume change (cell volumes from slide 13's lattice parameters):

\frac{\Delta V}{V} = \frac{140.6 - 134.2}{134.2} \approx +4.8\%, \qquad \text{plus a shear strain of about } 0.16
  • This expansion cracks the grains, so pure \mathrm{ZrO_2} cannot be made dense and sound: it is microcracked, weak, or falls apart.
  • At room temperature it is already monoclinic. No metastable t is left to transform at a crack tip, so the crack only breaks bonds and K_{IC} stays at a few \mathrm{MPa\,m^{1/2}}.

Design of Y-PSZ from Figure 02. \mathrm{Y^{3+}} on \mathrm{Zr^{4+}} sites creates oxygen vacancies (\mathrm{Y_2O_3} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Y_{Zr}^{\prime}} + 3\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}), which stabilise t and c.

  1. Composition: inside the t + c field but short of full stabilisation: x \approx 10 on the figure's axis (about 5 mol% \mathrm{Y_2O_3}, within the 3 to 8 mol% of slide 15).
  2. Solution treat at about 1950^\circ\mathrm{C}, just above the c boundary (about 1850 to 1900^\circ\mathrm{C} at x = 10): single-phase cubic grains. Cool fast to keep a supersaturated cubic solid solution.
  3. Age at about 1400^\circ\mathrm{C} in the t + c field: Y-lean t (about 3.5) precipitates as fine, coherent lenses in Y-rich c (about 14). By the lever rule
f_t = \frac{14.3 - 10}{14.3 - 3.5} \approx 0.40

Stop when the precipitates are just below the critical size, about 0.2\ \mu\mathrm{m}.

  1. Cool to room temperature. Below the eutectoid (about 560^\circ\mathrm{C}) the equilibrium is m + c, but the small, matrix-constrained t precipitates stay tetragonal: metastable t in a cubic matrix.

How this toughens. The tensile field of a crack supplies the missing driving force, so t particles in a zone of half-width w around the tip and faces transform to m. Their 4 to 5% expansion, held in by the matrix, puts the crack under compression (crack-tip shielding), and the transformation absorbs energy:

K_{tip} = K_{applied} - \Delta K_T, \qquad \Delta K_T \propto V_t\,\varepsilon^{T} E\,\sqrt{w}

The transformed wake grows as the crack advances (rising R-curve). K_{IC} rises from about 3\ \mathrm{MPa\,m^{1/2}} for cubic zirconia to 6 to 15\ \mathrm{MPa\,m^{1/2}} for PSZ, and strength rises too. More \mathrm{Y_2O_3} (8 mol% or more) gives fully stabilised cubic zirconia with nothing to transform.

• Class note pp 5 and 19 write D = \varepsilon_0\varepsilon_rP. The displacement is D = \varepsilon_0E + P = \varepsilon_0\varepsilon_rE (as the boxed line on p 19 has it); P itself is \varepsilon_0(\varepsilon_r - 1)E.

6a.html:
Given: A = 1.2\ \mathrm{cm^2} = 1.2\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}, d = 0.3\ \mathrm{mm} = 3.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m}, Q = 1.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{C}; at f = 1\ \mathrm{kHz}: \mathrm{BaTiO_3} \kappa = 1500, \tan\delta = 0.003; PZT \kappa = 1400, \tan\delta = 0.001; \varepsilon_0 = 8.854\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}.

Find: (i) the polarisation P in each dielectric, (ii) the dielectric loss current, (iii) the better material.

(i)

Solution. The free charge per unit plate area is the dielectric displacement. Since D = \varepsilon_0E + P = \kappa\varepsilon_0E:

\begin{aligned} D &= \frac{Q}{A} = \frac{1.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{C}}{1.2\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}} = 0.833\ \mathrm{C\,m^{-2}} \\ E &= \frac{D}{\kappa\varepsilon_0}, \qquad P = D - \varepsilon_0E = \varepsilon_0(\kappa - 1)E = D\,\frac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa} \end{aligned}
Quantity\mathrm{BaTiO_3}PZT
C = \kappa\varepsilon_0A/d5.31\ \mathrm{nF}4.96\ \mathrm{nF}
V = Q/C18.8\ \mathrm{kV}20.2\ \mathrm{kV}
E = V/d6.27\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}6.72\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}
P = D(\kappa - 1)/\kappa0.8328\ \mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}0.8327\ \mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}

Answer: P \approx 0.833\ \mathrm{C\,m^{-2}} (83\ \mu\mathrm{C\,cm^{-2}}) in both. The bound charge supplies 99.9% of the stored charge; PZT, with the lower \kappa, needs a 7% higher field.

(ii)

Solution. The loss current is the part of the AC current in phase with the voltage, I_L = \omega\varepsilon''E A = \sigma EA, with the dielectric conductivity \sigma = \omega\varepsilon_0\kappa\tan\delta and \omega = 2\pi(1000) = 6283\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}:

\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{BT}} &= (6283)(8.854\times10^{-12})(1500)(0.003) = 2.50\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{S\,m^{-1}} \\ I_{L,\mathrm{BT}} &= \sigma EA = (2.50\times10^{-7})(6.27\times10^{7})(1.2\times10^{-4}) = 1.88\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A} \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{PZT}} &= (6283)(8.854\times10^{-12})(1400)(0.001) = 7.79\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{S\,m^{-1}} \\ I_{L,\mathrm{PZT}} &= (7.79\times10^{-8})(6.72\times10^{7})(1.2\times10^{-4}) = 6.28\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{A} \end{aligned}

Check: the charging current is I_c = \omega CV = \omega Q = 0.628\ \mathrm{A} for both, and I_L = I_c\tan\delta.

Answer: I_L \approx 1.9\ \mathrm{mA} for \mathrm{BaTiO_3} and 0.63\ \mathrm{mA} for PZT.

(iii)

Both store the same charge with practically the same polarisation and charging current, so loss decides. PZT has one third of the loss current, so one third of the heat: average loss \tfrac12V_0I_L \approx 6.3\ \mathrm{W} against 17.7\ \mathrm{W}, and a quality factor 1/\tan\delta = 1000 against 333. Its cost is a 7% higher working voltage (20.2 against 18.8 kV). For either material the field, above 60\ \mathrm{MV\,m^{-1}}, is about five times the dielectric strength (12\ \mathrm{MV\,m^{-1}} for \mathrm{BaTiO_3}, slide 8), so a real part needs a thicker or multilayer dielectric.

Answer: choose PZT: equal charge storage with three times lower dielectric loss. \mathrm{BaTiO_3} would be preferred only if a lead-free part were required.

6b.html:
DLVO. Particles feel double-layer repulsion and van der Waals attraction (slide 39). For spheres of radius a at separation h \ll a:

V_T = V_R + V_A, \qquad V_A = -\frac{A\,a}{12h}, \qquad V_R = 2\pi\varepsilon_r\varepsilon_0\,a\,\psi_0^2\ln\left(1 + e^{-\kappa h}\right)

A: Hamaker constant; \psi_0: surface (zeta) potential; 1/\kappa: Debye length. A high barrier P1 means stable; with no barrier particles fall into the primary minimum M1 (coagulation); a shallow secondary minimum M2 gives reversible flocculation (slide 40).

  • Particle size. Both terms scale with a, so the barrier does too: in the figure's conditions about 170 kT at 0.25 \mum but only 7 kT at 10 nm. Very fine particles coagulate easily; coarse ones have higher barriers but deeper M2, and settle.
  • pH. \mathrm{H^+} and \mathrm{OH^-} set the charge relative to the IEP; V_R \propto \psi_0^2 is zero at the IEP, where attraction wins. Disperse alumina (IEP 8 to 9, slide 35) near pH 4 or 11.
  • Ionic strength. Salt, I = \tfrac{1}{2}\sum c_i z_i^2, compresses the double layer: 1/\kappa \approx 0.304/\sqrt{I} nm (water, 1:1, 25^\circ\mathrm{C}), 9.6 nm at 1 mM, 0.96 nm at 0.1 M. V_R shrinks, V_A does not, and the barrier vanishes above the critical coagulation concentration.
  • Electrolyte type. Counter-ion valence dominates: critical coagulation concentration \propto z^{-6} (Schulze-Hardy), so 1, 2 and 3-valent ions coagulate at 1 : 1/64 : 1/729. Adsorbing ions (\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}, phosphate, citrate) also lower or reverse \psi_0.

Hence a stable slip is far from the IEP, at low ionic strength, with monovalent ions.

Ionic strength compresses the double layer (1/\kappa \propto I^{-1/2}, about 10 nm at 1 mM), lowering the barrier to zero above the critical coagulation concentration

  • A barrier of about 15 to 25 kT is usually enough for practical stability; the figure's 170 kT at 1 mM is far above it.

6c.html:
Electrosteric stabilisation (slide 37): a polyelectrolyte dispersant such as ammonium polymethacrylate adsorbed on the particles.

  • Slip casting needs a concentrated (about 50 vol%), fluid, stable aqueous slip that packs uniformly against the plaster mould.
  • The charged polymer adds long-range electrostatic and short-range steric repulsion, so particles cannot reach the primary minimum even if the double layer is compressed.
  • Electrostatic alone is sensitive to pH and to ions leached from the powder and gypsum mould (\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}, \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}).
  • Steric alone needs a thick layer and much polymer; electrosteric works at below about 1 wt%.
pts: Chooses electrosteric stabilisation with a polyelectrolyte dispersant (credit steric stabilisation with an adsorbed polymer, the slide 36 example, if justified)
Reason: combined electrostatic and steric repulsion keeps a high-solids slip stable and fluid
Reason: tolerant of pH and ionic-strength changes (ions from powder and plaster mould), unlike electrostatic alone
Reason: needs less polymer than steric alone and suits water-based slips

7a(i-iii).html:
Given: T_{\mathrm{sor}} = 1200\ \mathrm{K}, T_{\mathrm{sub}} = 400\ \mathrm{K}, p_{\mathrm{back}} = 2.67\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{Pa}, H = 25\ \mathrm{cm}, ideal cosine emission, M = 65\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}, K_0^{\prime} = 159\ \mathrm{MPa}, h_{\mathrm{evap}} = 150{,}000\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}.

Find: (i) p_{\mathrm{eq}} at the source, (ii) the evaporation rate R_e, (iii) the flux F_{\mathrm{dep}} arriving at the substrate.

(i)

Solution. The vapour pressure rises exponentially with the source temperature. The heat of evaporation is per mole, so it goes with R:

\begin{aligned} p_{\mathrm{eq}} &= K_0^{\prime}\exp\left(-\frac{h_{\mathrm{evap}}}{RT_{\mathrm{sor}}}\right) \\ \frac{h_{\mathrm{evap}}}{RT_{\mathrm{sor}}} &= \frac{150{,}000\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}}{(8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}})(1200\ \mathrm{K})} = 15.03 \\ p_{\mathrm{eq}} &= (1.59\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{Pa})(2.95\times10^{-7}) = 47.0\ \mathrm{Pa} \end{aligned}

Answer: p_{\mathrm{eq}} \approx 47\ \mathrm{Pa} (0.35 Torr) at 1200 K.

(ii)

Solution. At equilibrium the evaporation flux equals the impingement flux of the vapour at p_{\mathrm{eq}} (Langmuir, Hertz-Knudsen), with an evaporation coefficient of 1. The mass of one atom is m = M/N_A:

\begin{aligned} m &= \frac{0.065\ \mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}}{6.022\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}} = 1.079\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg} \\ \frac{p_{\mathrm{back}}}{p_{\mathrm{eq}}} &= \frac{2.67\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{Pa}}{47.0\ \mathrm{Pa}} = 5.7\times10^{-4} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{return flux negligible} \\ R_e &= \frac{p_{\mathrm{eq}}}{\sqrt{2\pi m k T_{\mathrm{sor}}}} \\ \sqrt{2\pi m k T_{\mathrm{sor}}} &= \sqrt{2\pi\,(1.079\times10^{-25})(1.381\times10^{-23})(1200)} = 1.060\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}} \\ R_e &= \frac{47.0\ \mathrm{Pa}}{1.060\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}} = 4.43\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}} \end{aligned}

Check with the practical form: 3.513\times10^{22}\times 0.352/\sqrt{65 \times 1200} = 4.43\times10^{19}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}.

Answer: R_e \approx 4.4\times10^{23}\ \text{atoms}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}} (4.4\times10^{19}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}), that is 0.74\ \mathrm{mol\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}} or 0.048\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}.

(iii)

Solution. Ideal cosine emission means a small-area (planar) source. Its surface of constant flux is a sphere of diameter H that touches the source and the substrate, so the N_e = \bar{R}_e A_{\mathrm{sor}} atoms per second are spread over 4\pi(H/2)^2 = \pi H^2. With the printed hint \bar{R}_e \approx R_e, directly above the source:

\begin{aligned} F_{\mathrm{dep}} &= \frac{\bar{R}_e A_{\mathrm{sor}}}{\pi H^2} \approx \frac{R_e A_{\mathrm{sor}}}{\pi H^2} \\ \frac{F_{\mathrm{dep}}}{A_{\mathrm{sor}}} &= \frac{4.43\times10^{19}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}}{\pi\,(25\ \mathrm{cm})^2} = 2.26\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}\ \text{per}\ \mathrm{cm^2}\ \text{of source} \end{aligned}

The source area is not printed, so the flux is quoted per unit source area; for A_{\mathrm{sor}} = 1\ \mathrm{cm^2}, F_{\mathrm{dep}} \approx 2.3\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}.

Line-of-sight check: p_{\mathrm{back}} = 2.0\times10^{-4} Torr, so \lambda \approx 5\times10^{-3}/(2.0\times10^{-4}) = 25\ \mathrm{cm} \approx H: transport is only just collision-free.

Answer: F_{\mathrm{dep}} \approx 2.3\times10^{16}\,A_{\mathrm{sor}}\ \text{atoms}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}, with A_{\mathrm{sor}} in \mathrm{cm^2}.

7b.fix: Class note p 6 says electronic polarisation "operates at very high frequencies, > 10^{15} Hz". It operates at all frequencies up to about 10^{15} Hz (its ultraviolet resonance) and is lost above that, so \varepsilon_r \to 1 at X-ray frequencies, as the note's own curve on p 10 shows.
7b.html:
The total polarisation is the sum of four contributions, so

P = P_e + P_i + P_d + P_s, \qquad \varepsilon_r - 1 = \chi_e + \chi_i + \chi_d + \chi_s

Each mechanism adds to \varepsilon_r only while its charges can follow the alternating field. The heavier the moving unit and the longer the distance it moves, the lower the frequency at which it drops out: f_{\mathrm{interfacial}} < f_{\mathrm{dipolar}} < f_{\mathrm{ionic}} < f_{\mathrm{electronic}}.

MechanismWhat movesSize of contributionActive up to
Space charge (interfacial)mobile ions or electrons drift to grain boundaries, pores, electrodesvery large in impure, porous ceramicsabout 10^{2} to 10^{3} Hz
Dipolar (orientation)permanent dipoles rotate or switch (\mathrm{H_2O}, off-centre \mathrm{Ti^{4+}})large: water 80, \mathrm{BaTiO_3} thousands10^{7} to 10^{9} Hz (radio, microwave)
Ioniccations and anions shift on their elastic bondsa few unitsabout 10^{13} Hz (infrared)
Electronicelectron cloud shifts against the nucleussmall, in every material; \varepsilon_r = n^2about 10^{15} Hz (ultraviolet)

Frequency ranges.

  • At low frequency (below about 100 Hz) all four act, so \varepsilon_r' is highest.
  • Space charge fails first (a relaxation step), then dipolar orientation in the radio to microwave range.
  • In the infrared only ionic and electronic remain; at the ionic resonance \varepsilon_r' swings and drops.
  • At optical frequencies only electronic polarisation remains, so \varepsilon_r = n^2. Above about 10^{16} Hz none can follow and \varepsilon_r \to 1.

Loss. At each relaxation or resonance the polarisation lags the field, so the loss \varepsilon'' (and \tan\delta = \varepsilon''/\varepsilon') peaks there. The microwave oven works at the dipolar relaxation of water.

Evidence. Comparing the static \varepsilon_r with n^2 separates the terms: diamond 5.7 against 5.85 (electronic only), NaCl 5.9 against 2.37 (ionic adds about 3.5), water 80 against 1.77 (dipolar dominates).

Dipolar: rotation of permanent dipoles, large contribution, relaxes at about 10^{7} to 10^{9} Hz (radio to microwave)
Ionic: relative shift of cations and anions, contributes up to the infrared resonance near 10^{13} Hz
Electronic: electron cloud shift in every material, up to about 10^{15} Hz, giving \varepsilon_r = n^2 at optical frequencies and \varepsilon_r \to 1 beyond

  • Dipolar and space-charge losses are relaxations (broad peaks, no overshoot); ionic and electronic are resonances (sharp, with \varepsilon' swinging above and below).
  • Diamond's n^2 (5.85) slightly exceeds its static value (5.7) because n is measured at visible frequency, just below the electronic resonance; within error they are the same.

Each \mathrm{Zn_i^{\bullet\bullet}} releases two electrons, so electroneutrality is 2[\mathrm{Zn_i^{\bullet\bullet}}] = [n^{\prime}] and n = (2K)^{1/3}p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/6}, not (K/2)^{1/3}p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/6}. The -1/6 exponent, and so the slide's conclusion, is unchanged.
8a.html:
Annealing at low p_{\mathrm{O_2}} pulls oxygen out of an oxide. It raises the conductivity only if the defects it creates supply the oxide's majority carriers. ZnO is a metal-excess n-type oxide; CuO is a metal-deficient p-type oxide.

ZnO: donors and free electrons. Oxygen leaves and the excess Zn sits as interstitial donors:

\mathrm{ZnO} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Zn_i^{\bullet}} + e^{\prime} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2(g)}, \qquad K_1 = [\mathrm{Zn_i^{\bullet}}]\,n\,p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{1/2}

With electroneutrality n = [\mathrm{Zn_i^{\bullet}}]:

n = K_1^{1/2}\,p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/4}

This is the measured slope for ZnO. Oxygen vacancies, \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}} + 2e^{\prime} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2(g)}, act the same way (n \propto p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/6}). Zn has no lower stable valence, so the electrons go into the conduction band and are mobile: \sigma = ne\mu_n rises, about tenfold for four decades lower p_{\mathrm{O_2}}.

CuO: holes from Cu vacancies. Its carriers come from oxygen uptake:

\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_{Cu}^{\prime\prime}} + 2h^{\bullet}, \qquad K_2 = \frac{[\mathrm{V_{Cu}^{\prime\prime}}]\,p^2}{p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{1/2}}

With p = 2[\mathrm{V_{Cu}^{\prime\prime}}]:

p = (2K_2)^{1/3}\,p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{+1/6}

Low p_{\mathrm{O_2}} drives this reaction backwards: it can only remove holes. Electrons released by oxygen loss do not become free carriers:

e^{\prime} + h^{\bullet} \rightarrow \text{null}, \qquad \mathrm{Cu_{Cu}^{\times}} + e^{\prime} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu_{Cu}^{\prime}}\ (\mathrm{Cu^{+}})

They annihilate holes or are trapped on reducible Cu as slow small polarons. The anneal only moves CuO towards stoichiometry, with a weak 1/6 power, so \sigma stays almost unchanged (or falls slightly).

Nanoparticle surfaces. Low p_{\mathrm{O_2}} also desorbs chemisorbed \mathrm{O^-}, which traps electrons in the ZnO depletion layer; this adds to the rise. On p-type CuO the same oxygen gives a hole-accumulation layer, so its loss cannot help.

Conclusion: the defects made by reduction are the majority-carrier source in n-type ZnO but compensating defects in p-type CuO. To raise \sigma of CuO, anneal at higher p_{\mathrm{O_2}} or dope with an acceptor such as \mathrm{Li_{Cu}^{\prime}}.

8b.html:
Structural features that let \mathrm{BaTiO_3} store more charge

  1. Perovskite cage. Large \mathrm{Ba^{2+}} (0.136 nm) and \mathrm{O^{2-}} form a close-packed framework, and the big \mathrm{Ba^{2+}} expands the oxygen octahedron. The small \mathrm{Ti^{4+}} (0.064 nm, r_{\mathrm{Ti}}/r_{\mathrm{O}} = 0.44, just above the 0.414 limit for six-fold sites) is loose in it: the "rattling" titanium ion.
  2. Permanent dipoles. Below \theta_c = 120^\circ\mathrm{C} the \mathrm{Ti^{4+}} shifts off-centre along [001] by about 6 pm and the \mathrm{O^{2-}} ions move the other way (6 to 9 pm). The cell becomes tetragonal (c/a \approx 4.03/3.98 = 1.01) and every cell carries a dipole: spontaneous polarisation P_s \approx 0.27\ \mathrm{C\,m^{-2}} in a single crystal.
  3. Switchable domains. Neighbouring dipoles couple into domains with thin, low-energy 90° and 180° walls. A small field flips \mathrm{Ti^{4+}} between its two off-centre minima and moves the walls, so P changes greatly per unit field.
  4. Result. Orientation (dipolar) polarisation adds to the ionic and electronic terms, giving \kappa \approx 1500 to 5000 against 4 to 10 for linear ceramics (\mathrm{Al_2O_3} about 9). \kappa rises to about 10^{4} near \theta_c, where the wells are shallow, and to about 5000 at a grain size near 1 µm (slide 12).

Frequency range. The \mathrm{Ti^{4+}} switching and domain-wall polarisation, which gives the high \kappa, follows the field from DC to about 10^{9} Hz (little change until the GHz range). Ionic polarisation continues to about 10^{13} Hz (infrared) and electronic to about 10^{15} Hz (ultraviolet); at optical frequencies \varepsilon_r \approx n^2 \approx 5.8. Space charge at grain boundaries adds below about 10^{3} Hz. So \mathrm{BaTiO_3} polarises from DC to about 10^{15} Hz but is a high-\kappa dielectric only up to microwaves.

Crystal structure and loop shape (Figure 04). A loop needs switchable permanent dipoles, so only the non-centrosymmetric phases show one. The depth of the \mathrm{Ti^{4+}} double well sets the coercive field E_c; the off-centre shift sets P_s and P_r.

  • (a) 90 °C: still tetragonal but close to \theta_c. The shift and c/a are smaller and the wells shallow, so the loop is slim: small P_r and E_c, steep slope (high \kappa).
  • (b) 120 °C: the cell becomes cubic (m3m) with \mathrm{Ti^{4+}} central and no permanent dipole. The material is paraelectric, P = \varepsilon_0\chi E, and the loop collapses into a line through the origin with no remanence.
  • At room temperature and in the orthorhombic and rhombohedral phases (below 5 and -90^\circ\mathrm{C}) the wells are deeper, so the loops are fatter, with larger E_c.

The loop area (the switching energy) therefore shrinks as T \to \theta_c and vanishes in the cubic phase.

8b.watch:
• The 120 °C trace may still show a hair-thin opening: the transition is first order, so right at \theta_c a field can induce the polar phase. A few degrees higher the response is linear.
  • Carter calls the mechanism in \mathrm{BaTiO_3} dipolar (permanent dipoles being oriented); some texts call it ionic because the dipoles come from ion shifts. Name it and say why.
  • A polycrystalline ceramic has a higher E_c and a lower P_r than a single crystal (E_c = 0.1\ \mathrm{MV\,m^{-1}}, P_s = 0.27\ \mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}), because grains clamp each other and 90° domains resist switching.
  • Room temperature is far below the \kappa peak at 120 °C, which is why capacitor grades shift \theta_c with \mathrm{Sr^{2+}} (BST) or use fine grains.
